notes: Leasehold enfranchisement preliminary issue; statutory qualifying tenant definition applied to single lease of entire block.

enrichment.short_title: Maurice v Holloware: qualifying tenant status under single block lease

statutes_considered.title: Leasehold Reform Housing and Urban Development Act 1993

key_facts: Trustees of a charitable foundation owned a block of 28 flats in London and held the entire building under one 80-year lease expiring in about 12 years.
Defendants served notices under the 1993 Act requiring new 90-year leases at a peppercorn rent for all 28 flats.
The claimants disputed entitlement on the sole remaining ground that the defendants were not qualifying tenants because they held all flats under one lease covering common parts as well as flats.
After grant of new leases the existing lease would continue in part for the residual common parts.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Preliminary issue on meaning of qualifying tenant before leasehold valuation tribunal proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Claimants' objection rejected; defendants held to be qualifying tenants entitled to new leases for all flats.
enrichment.ratio: A tenant holding all flats under one long lease is a qualifying tenant of each flat under sections 39 and 101 of the 1993 Act; new leases are granted in substitution for the existing lease to the extent of the demised flats, with rent apportionment at common law for the residual lease.
legal_issues: Whether tenants of all flats under one lease qualify for collective enfranchisement notices
Whether section 56(1) substitution requires surrender of the entire existing lease
How rent under the residual lease should be apportioned after grant of flat leases
Whether service charge mechanisms adequately protect the landlord's interests

notes: School permanent exclusion JR; inadequate decision letter quashed though clerk presence ground failed.

enrichment.short_title: R (AI) v G College IAP: quashing exclusion for inadequate reasons
key_facts: A GCSE student was permanently excluded after slapping and head-butting a fellow pupil on 20 September 2004, an incident captured on mobile phone video.
An independent appeal panel dismissed his appeal in a two-sentence decision letter that did not explain whether a prior temporary exclusion or parental non-involvement were considered.
The claimant sought judicial review on due process, inadequate reasons and failure to consider proximity of GCSE exams.
Bennett J granted permission on grounds 2 and 3 but refused ground 1 concerning the clerk's role.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Expedited judicial review of a permanent school exclusion upheld by an independent appeal panel.
enrichment.outcome: Decision quashed for inadequate reasons and remitted to a freshly constituted panel; half costs awarded to the claimant; leave to appeal refused on clerk attendance ground.
enrichment.ratio: Decision letters on school exclusions must give sufficient detail for parties to understand why exclusion was upheld; later witness statements that contradict or materially expand cryptic reasons cannot cure a failure to give adequate reasons at the time of decision.
legal_issues: Whether the appeal panel's two-sentence reasons were adequate
Whether later clarification by the panel chair could validate the decision
Whether presence and advice of a clerk at a private exclusion appeal was unlawful
Whether permanent exclusion shortly before GCSE exams required explicit reasoning

notes: Part 8 rent review dispute; head lease not surrendered and 1999 review held invalid for time.

enrichment.short_title: Vowles v Aston: surrender construction and rent review time limits
key_facts: Subtenants of Longdon Heath Sawmills sought declarations on validity of a rent review under a 1975 head lease linked to their underlease rent.
Landlords served rent review notices in October and December 1998 but an arbitrator wrongly treated late notice as non-fatal because of 'either/or' construction of clause 2.3.
On 18 October 2000 Kenyan Securities assigned its interest back to the freeholder landlords in an 'Assignment in Release' with a separate Declaration of Trust.
The subtenant argued the assignment operated as an express surrender extinguishing the head lease and any accrued rent review right.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part 8 claim for declarations on rent review validity and effect of 2000 assignment, following arbitration on timing issues.
enrichment.outcome: Head lease not surrendered on 18 October 2000; 1999 rent review machinery not validly operated because time was of the essence and waiver not proved; declarations made accordingly.
enrichment.ratio: The word 'surrender' in a recital is ambiguous where operative clauses release the assignee personally from future and past liabilities without extinguishing the term; commercial context favours construction as personal release rather than technical surrender, and all rent review time stipulations are of the essence under clause 2.5.
legal_issues: Whether the October 2000 assignment effected surrender of the head lease
Whether a separate Declaration of Trust could be used to construe the assignment
Whether the arbitrator errored in treating 'or' in clause 2.3 as permitting late notice
Whether the subtenant was a party entitled to appeal the arbitrator's decision

Chambers v Kingham (1877) 3 Ch D 251
Mannai Investment Co Ltd v Eagle Star Life Assurance Co Ltd [1997] AC 749

notes: Permission refused on contact appeal; litigants in person cooperated in flawed but fair trial process.

enrichment.short_title: Re D: procedural fairness of contact trial with late CAFCASS report
key_facts: Parents disputed contact with their daughter S in proceedings transferred from Newport to Cardiff when the allocated judge was conflicted out.
The CAFCASS officer's report was significantly late and an addendum report was served only days before the one-day trial on 24 June 2004.
Neither parent properly served witness statements by the extended deadline; each attended trial without having read the other's statement.
The judge refused to hear further partner witnesses to avoid overrunning the time estimate and completed the hearing in one day.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Oral permission application to appeal from a county court contact order, directed by Black J on procedural fairness grounds only.
enrichment.outcome: Permission refused; appeal not heard; no order for costs.
enrichment.ratio: Alleged procedural unfairness from late CAFCASS reporting and unserved statements is not established where the appellant cooperated throughout the trial without raising objections and an experienced judge managed a one-day hearing between litigants in person fairly.
legal_issues: Whether late CAFCASS reporting denied a fair opportunity to prepare
Whether failure to exchange statements before trial rendered the hearing unfair
Whether refusal to hear partner witnesses showed judicial impatience or prejudice
Whether procedural complaints must be raised at trial to support an appeal

notes: Gypsy caravan planning permission; split court adjourned renewed permission to three judges.

enrichment.short_title: Smith v SoS: gypsy caravan site planning permission appeal adjourned
key_facts: A Romany Gypsy applicant sought planning permission for caravans and access at Woodside Caravan Park in Bedfordshire for his extended family.
An inspector refused permission in a decision letter of 23 July 2004 and Sullivan J dismissed the section 288 appeal on 29 October 2004.
Four grounds of challenge were renewed on a further permission application, including alleged reliance on proximity to other authorised sites and a 'shift' of caravans to unauthorised sites.
Laws and Sedley LJJ disagreed on whether arguable points of law warranted permission.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed oral permission application to appeal Sullivan J's dismissal of a section 288 planning appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Permission application adjourned to a court of three with appeal to follow if granted; half-day time estimate.
enrichment.ratio: Where two members of the Court of Appeal divide on whether planning inspector reasoning raises arguable errors of law, particularly as to legally relevant considerations in gypsy site cases, the appropriate course is to adjourn permission to a full court rather than finally refusing or granting leave on the papers alone.
legal_issues: Whether proximity to other gypsy sites and risk of community conflict is a relevant planning consideration
Whether a trend of caravans moving from authorised to unauthorised sites can justify refusal
Whether the inspector's cumulative reasoning on a strong application was legally flawed
Whether Sullivan J correctly rejected all grounds of challenge

notes: Commercial Court summary judgment; binding settlement letter and caveat email read together.

enrichment.short_title: Cable & Wireless v Valentine: binding Foulger liability agreement with Willis
key_facts: C&W and captive insurer Pender sued Willis and others over an alleged fraud diverting premium income through employee Peter Foulger.
On the eve of a case management conference Willis's group counsel agreed a signed letter accepting vicarious liability for Foulger's acts to avoid being joined.
Bowden's signed letter was qualified by an email stating Willis accepted legal responsibility only for a fair share of damages, not 100 percent of losses.
Garard accepted the caveat in a telephone call and countersigned the letter; Willis's UK lawyers then denied any binding agreement.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Cross-applications for summary judgment on whether a binding settlement agreement existed ahead of joinder at a CMC.
enrichment.outcome: Binding agreement held on terms of the signed letter, caveat email and 25 November telephone conversation; Willis's summary judgment application failed.
enrichment.ratio: A signed letter of agreement and contemporaneous qualifying email can constitute a binding contract where the offeree accepts the qualification; acceptance of liability for a just and equitable share of loss under the 1978 Act is sufficiently certain without an obligation to negotiate in good faith.
legal_issues: Whether Bowden's caveat email prevented contract formation
Whether liability for a 'fair share' was too uncertain to enforce
Whether an obligation to negotiate quantum rendered the agreement unenforceable
Whether Willis was bound to accept Foulger's acts and facts for deferred joinder purposes

notes: Family appeals dismissed; joint residence division and periodical payments held unappealable.

enrichment.short_title: Re W: permission refused on children and ancillary relief orders
key_facts: Following acrimonious separation the judge made a joint residence order dividing time between parents for children L and S, with L estranged from her mother.
The judge imposed a discretionary division of time not advocated by the CAFCASS officer or either parent; the parties later varied arrangements by consent.
The judge ordered the father to pay £1,000 per month periodical payments and half the wife's ancillary relief costs.
The father appealed criticising procedural handling of CAFCASS evidence, a comment calling him stupid, and reliance on an FDR obstruction note.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Oral permission applications to appeal children and financial orders made at county court trial.
enrichment.outcome: Permission refused on all grounds; appeal dismissed with costs to the respondent.
enrichment.ratio: A judge may impose a joint residence time division without prior consultation where it remains a discretionary detail under a joint order; unjudicial remarks and FDR obstruction records do not establish bias; periodical payments and costs awards within a wide discretion are not appealable merely because harsh.
legal_issues: Whether the judge erred by imposing a residence division without putting it to CAFCASS or parties
Whether calling the father a stupid man showed prejudgment
Whether an FDR record of obstructive conduct improperly influenced the financial award
Whether £12,000 annual periodical payments and 50 percent costs were outside permissible discretion

notes: CPR 19.5(3)(b) appeal dismissed; Trust joinder not necessary to pursue surgeon claim.

enrichment.short_title: Martin v Kaisary: joinder of hospital trust after limitation refused
key_facts: After private prostate surgery by consultant Mr Kaisary the claimant suffered cardiac arrest and permanent brain damage from post-operative bleeding.
Proceedings were issued against Mr Kaisary alone two to three days before limitation expired; particulars alleged vicarious liability for hospital staff negligence.
Mr Kaisary denied vicarious liability for nursing and medical staff; the claimant applied under CPR 19.5 to add the Royal Free Hospital Trust after limitation.
Simon J refused joinder under rule 19.5(3)(b) and the claimant appealed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from refusal to add a defendant under CPR 19.5 after expiry of the primary limitation period.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; addition of the Trust held unnecessary because the claim against Mr Kaisary could proceed without determining hospital staff negligence.
enrichment.ratio: Under CPR 19.5(3)(b) a new party may be added after limitation only if the claim cannot properly be carried on against the original party without joinder; determining a surgeon's liability does not require joining the employer to adjudicate staff negligence when factual evidence of staff conduct can be obtained without making them defendants.
legal_issues: Whether CPR 19.5(3)(b) permits adding the NHS trust to pursue alternative negligence claims
Whether the claim against Mr Kaisary required determination of hospital staff liability
Whether mistaken belief in vicarious liability could support substitution under rule 19.5(3)(a)
How section 35 of the Limitation Act constrains the rule-making power behind CPR 19.5

notes: Section 25 MHA barring review; dangerousness not addressed in original reasons.

enrichment.short_title: Oldcorn v West London MH Trust: unlawful section 25 barring review
key_facts: A paranoid schizophrenic patient detained under section 3 was subject to a nearest relative discharge request assigned to his father.
The responsible medical officer barred discharge under section 25 and hospital managers upheld detention on 30 April 2004.
Written reasons focused on illness and medication compliance but did not address whether discharge would likely cause dangerousness to others or himself.
The review form's dangerousness boxes were unticked and the chairman later supplemented reasons after a challenge was threatened.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a hospital managers' review upholding a section 25 barring order.
enrichment.outcome: Decision declared unlawful for failure to give legally sufficient reasons addressing dangerousness; subsequent supplementation rejected; costs awarded.
enrichment.ratio: Where a nearest relative seeks discharge under section 23, a section 25 barring order requires explicit consideration and reasoning on dangerousness; reasons must be given at the time of decision and later supplementation cannot cure omission of a statutory condition essential to legality.
legal_issues: Whether the panel adequately considered section 25 dangerousness criteria
Whether later chairman statements could validate the original decision
Whether common law requires reasons where personal liberty is at stake
Whether defective detention may give rise to Article 5 damages

notes: ASBO and possession appeal; defective process led to undertakings substituted for ASBOs.

enrichment.short_title: Moat Housing v Harris: ASBOs set aside after defective without-notice process
key_facts: A registered social landlord sought possession and ASBOs against a tenant family in Liphook after allegations of anti-social behaviour on the estate.
On 29 October 2004 the landlord attended the home at about 9 pm with police and a television crew, serving court papers including injunction orders wrongly naming other parties.

County court ASBOs and a possession order followed; the Court of Appeal criticised use of without-notice procedures, hearsay evidence and failure to identify post-2002 conduct to the criminal standard.
Serious findings against the adults largely rested on events of a single night rather than persistent serious anti-social behaviour.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from possession order and ASBOs made at Southampton County Court, with related challenge to earlier without-notice injunction process.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals allowed in part; ASBOs set aside and replaced with undertakings or ASBIs without time limit; procedural and evidential defects in the without-notice process condemned.
enrichment.ratio: ASBOs require necessity to protect the public from further anti-social acts, precise terms, recorded findings of fact and fair process; without-notice injunctions must strictly comply with procedural requirements and anonymous hearsay cannot support ASBOs without findings to the criminal standard on conduct after the statutory commencement date.
legal_issues: Lawfulness of without-notice anti-social behaviour injunctions served at the tenant's home
Whether ASBOs were necessary given conduct of the adults versus children
Whether hearsay and anonymous complaints satisfied the criminal standard of proof
Whether possession and ASBO procedure complied with Articles 6 and 8 ECHR
linked_authorities: R (McCann) v Manchester Crown Court [2002] UKHL 39
R v P (Shane Tony) [2004] EWCA Crim 287
R v Manchester Crown Court ex parte McCann [2002] UKHL 39
